qs.q: A 50-year-old smoker is found to have a 3.5 cm asymptomatic solid renal mass incidentally discovered during an abdominal ultrasound for biliary colic. What is the most appropriate initial imaging step to properly characterise this lesion and assess local staging?
o: Routine core needle biopsy of the mass prior to any surgical intervention
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Plain abdominal radiography with intravenous urography for visualization
Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging without intravenous contrast agents
qs.e: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the main investigation to characterise an enhancing solid mass, assess its size, local extent, renal vein and IVC involvement, and check for metastasis. Routine biopsy is avoided due to seeding risk.

qs.q: What is the first‑line imaging modality for a patient presenting with suspected biliary colic?
qs.e: Ultrasound is rapid, non‑invasive, and detects gallstones and gallbladder wall changes. MRCP, CT, and HIDA are reserved for further evaluation.

es.q: List and explain the clinical features that differentiate biliary colic from acute cholecystitis.
es.m:
**Differentiating features**:
- **Biliary colic**: sudden, steady pain in epigastrium/RUQ after a fatty meal, builds over 15–60 min, lasts 1–5 h, resolves; no fever, normal temperature, mild epigastric tenderness, no Murphy’s sign.
- **Acute cholecystitis**: continuous severe RUQ pain radiating to right scapula/shoulder, fever and tachycardia, positive Murphy’s sign, guarding, palpable gallbladder, possible mild jaundice.
- Nausea/vomiting present in both but more pronounced in cholecystitis.
- Leukocytosis and raised CRP are typical of cholecystitis, usually absent in biliary colic.

ai.title: Biliary Colic
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Transient obstruction of the cystic or common bile duct by a gallstone causes severe, episodic RUQ pain after fatty meals. Pain lasts 15‑60 min, resolves as the stone moves, with minimal systemic signs.

sections.p: Biliary colic is pain from a gallstone temporarily blocking the cystic duct (or CBD). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging that shows stones without signs of inflammation.
b: Stone seen on ultrasound or plain abdominal X‑ray
Normal temperature, white cell count, and no Murphy’s sign during pain‑free interval

sections.p: Severity is graded by pain intensity, duration, and impact on vitals. No formal staging system exists; clinicians categorize as uncomplicated colic versus complicated (e.g., cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis).
b: Uncomplicated: pain resolves, labs normal
Complicated: persistent pain >6 h, fever, jaundice, elevated LFTs

sections.p: Gallstones are the dominant cause; in low‑resource settings, pigment stones from chronic hemolysis (sickle cell, malaria) are common.
b: Cholesterol stones – obesity, high‑fat diet, female, fertile, forty
Pigment stones – hemolysis (sickle cell, malaria), infection, cirrhosis

sections.p: Sudden RUQ or epigastric pain after a fatty meal, lasting 15 min to 5 h, often radiating to the right shoulder or scapula. Associated nausea, vomiting, sweating, and restlessness.
b: Pain peaks within 30 min, then slowly subsides
No fever, no jaundice, normal bowel sounds

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm stones and exclude complications.

t.b: Detects gallstones, assesses gallbladder wall, looks for CBD dilation – positive confirms stone; normal wall rules out acute cholecystitis

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin)
t.b: Identify CBD obstruction or cholangitis – normal values support uncomplicated colic
Rule out pancreatitis when pain radiates to the back – normal levels favour biliary colic

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable: bedside gallbladder scan with portable probe or plain abdominal X‑ray (detects radiopaque sto
t.b: Provides indirect evidence; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and refer for imaging when possible

sections.p: Progression to infection or obstruction requires urgent care.
b: Fever >38 °C or leukocytosis → acute cholecystitis
Jaundice or bilirubin >2 mg/dL → choledocholithiasis
Pain >6 h, hypotension, tachycardia → possible perforation or pancreatitis

sections.p: Treat pain, prevent recurrence, and arrange definitive stone removal.
b: Analgesia: IV paracetamol ± short‑acting opioid (e.g., morphine) for severe pain; avoid NSAIDs if renal insufficiency or active ulcer disease
Antiemetics: ondansetron or metoclopramide for nausea
Hydration: IV crystalloids if vomiting or dehydration
Definitive: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy once pain-free; in low‑resource settings, open cholecystectomy may be used
If CBD stones suspected and ERCP unavailable, consider surgical CBD exploration

sections.p: Schedule surgery within 6‑8 weeks after the last episode. Counsel on diet and risk factors.
b: Low‑fat diet, weight control, avoid rapid weight loss
Screen for hemolytic disorders in recurrent pigment stones
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce future liver disease

sections.p: Conditions that cause RUQ pain but have different pathophysiology.
b: Acute cholecystitis – persistent pain, positive Murphy’s sign, fever
Choledocholithiasis – jaundice, elevated bilirubin, CBD dilation
Peptic ulcer disease – epigastric pain related to meals, no radiation to shoulder

sections.p: Normal tests do not exclude stone disease.
b: Ultrasound may miss small CBD stones; consider MRCP if suspicion remains
LFTs can be normal in early obstruction; repeat if symptoms persist

faq.q: Why is Murphy’s sign usually absent in biliary colic?
faq.a: The stone only blocks the cystic duct temporarily; the gallbladder wall is not inflamed, so palpation does not elicit pain.

faq.q: Can a normal ultrasound rule out biliary colic?
faq.a: No; small stones or CBD stones can be missed. Clinical correlation is essential.
When colic progresses to acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis, indicated by fever, jaundice, or rising enzymes.

exam: What bedside findings differentiate biliary colic from acute cholecystitis? — Absence of Murphy’s sign, normal temperature, and transient pain that resolves.
A patient with RUQ pain after a fatty meal has normal LFTs but ultrasound shows a stone. What is the next step? — Provide analgesia, antiemetics, and arrange elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
How would you manage a patient with suspected biliary colic in a hospital without ultrasound? — Base decision on classic history, give analgesia, monitor vitals, and refer for imaging when available.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in a patient with suspected biliary colic who also has chronic kidney disease? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function; use paracetamol and opioids instead.
What red‑flag symptom would change your diagnosis from biliary colic to choledocholithiasis? — Development of jaundice or bilirubin >2 mg/dL.
Explain why pigment stones are more common in sickle‑cell disease in East Africa. — Chronic hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, promoting calcium bilirubinate stone formation.

A patient presents with RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder but no fever. What investigations are essential and why? — Ultrasound to locate stones; LFTs to rule out CBD obstruction; amylase/lipase to exclude pancreatitis.

What is the rationale for elective rather than emergency cholecystectomy in uncomplicated biliary colic? — The inflammation is absent, allowing safe scheduling; emergency surgery carries higher morbidity.
